articles.content_orig:
President Trump has reportedly rejected a seven-day cease-fire proposed by Iran and expects to resume bombing the country after the midterm elections.
As part of the proposed cease-fire, Tehran pledged to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations on dismantling its nuclear program in exchange for the US ending its blockade of Iranian ports.
However, Trump is “skeptical” Iran will agree to his demands and has told aides it is “likely” the US military restarts airstrikes after the November contests, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing US officials.
It’s unclear what level of strikes Trump is planning on launching.
In his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week, Trump warned that with peace negotiations stalled, he could choose to “annihilate” Iran.
The White House did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

articles.content_orig:
At the conclusion of Xi's visit, CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer if the leaders achieved anything new on artificial intelligence.
"I wouldn't say anything new," Greer said. I mean, we've established this this dialogue, AI dialogue with the Chinese, which really is when I think about it, I think of like the red phone between the Kremlin and the White House during the Cold War. And the AI dialogue at a minimum is an opportunity, if the sides feel like they have something they need to share, whether it's risks or other things, we can do it. Most important thing is having a channel."
Greer said there would be "another meeting on AI in the next month or so" although the agenda has not yet been set.
Though Mr. Trump declined to answer shouted questions from reporters about Taiwan during Xi's visit, U.S. ambassador to China David Perdue insisted there is "no change" in the United States' policy toward Taiwan.
" There's no change, no change in the Taiwan policy here," Perdue told CNBC Friday. "He's fully committed to the One China policy. We're committed to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiques, and the six assurances. Nothing has changed there. Of course, China has tried to coerce change in that regard. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there."
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."

articles.title_orig: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
articles.title_zh: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
articles.content_orig:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.
Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.
"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.
Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic".
The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.
It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.
"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.
He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".
"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.
A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".
Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached
The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief.
It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements.
But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes.
Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.
The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.
Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz.
Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters.
However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula.
The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.
The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations. US media has reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has requested military support from Trump.
During his speech at the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
On Friday, Araghchi said Iran did not accept "coercion, threats or intimidation" and added that "peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation".

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court lets Trump administration use revamped federal voter eligibility database for now
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court lets Trump administration use revamped federal voter eligibility database for now
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.
The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful.
Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls.
But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters.
On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship.
The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said.
In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked.
In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added.
Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act.
The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement.
Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision.
The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement.
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security.
The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections.
The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches.
After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune .
Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen.
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion.
In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters.
Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system.
Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.
Jane C. Timm is a senior reporter for NBC News.

By JON BRADY, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER
Published: 10:23 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 10:57 EDT, 25 September 2026
Rory Stewart says his family told him to switch off his social media after his viral appearance on Newsnight that saw him spin and stare intensely at a female journalist.
Former MP turned podcaster Mr Stewart, 53, gave a whole new meaning to political spin with his violent pivot to the New Statesman's Ailbhe Rea last week.
A clip of the one-time Tory leadership challenger's bizarre swivel, aired on September 18, became a sensation on social media this week.
But Mr Stewart, best known now as one of the co-hosts of The Rest Is Politics alongside former Labour spin doctor Alastair Campbell, has maintained his silence on it – until now.
In a clip posted to Newsnight's TikTok account the politician – who was wearing an unexplained plaster on his face – said in a clip filmed today that he had been abroad since the show had gone out.
He added that he had been under the orders of his family to disable social media on his phone.
'I'm just coming back from abroad and I've missed all of this because I was on an Army base and then I've been away,' he said in the clip, filmed in the back of a car.
'And, under strict instructions from my family I have disabled all social media on this phone.'
Rory Stewart has responded to his viral Newsnight moment after days of silence - revealing he had been told to silence his social media
His sudden spin to political journalist Ailbhe Rea became an overnight sensation when it was shared on X
The former Tory leadership contender used the video as an opportunity to re-enact the dramatic spin, suggesting he has seen the funny side
Wrapping it up, he said:  'I don't know what to say - thank you, and I guess all I can do is this.' He then pulled off the head swivel once again, suggesting he has seen the funny side.
Reacting to the video, viewers appear to have chalked it up as another eccentric moment from Mr Stewart, who gained a reputation as a well-meaning but quirky oddball during his time in politics.
'Rory is a loveable eccentric - I'm not sure what the problem is,' said one viewer, while another said: 'He clearly just didn't realise he was on camera.'
'Come on, you cannot hate this man,' added a third commenter.
While he has acknowledged his viral moment, Mr Stewart did not explain exactly why he turned so suddenly to Ms Rea, political editor of the New Statesman.
He had just finished responding to a question on his attendance at the King's artificial intelligence summit earlier this month, branding the notion of British society depending wholly on US and Chinese-owned AI firms 'terrifying'.
As Ms Rea was prompted for her own thoughts by the host, former Daily Mail online political editor Matt Chorley, Mr Stewart turned and leaned intensely towards Ms Rea, who did not appear to react.
A two-second clip of the moment was posted on X earlier this week, where metrics suggest it has been seen 17 million times, picking up 23,000 likes.
The former Army officer and diplomat's rapid twirl was compared by witty users to, among other things, a jackknifing lorry and a labrador hearing the opening of a bag of crisps.
Reaction to the clip was merciless, with Mr Stewart compared to an attentive dog and a jackknifing lorry. Ms Rea has seen the funny side (pictured)
While veteran political journalist Ms Rea did not immediately acknowledge Mr Stewart's potent pirouette in the studio, she has since joked about the moment online.
Promoting an article on X on Thursday, she published a GIF of the moment Mr Stewart spun to look at her, captioning it: 'By the way I would please like attention levels like this on my latest interview.'
Mr Stewart developed a reputation for endearing eccentricity and nerdiness during his time in Parliament, particularly as he ran in the 2019 Tory leadership contest ultimately won by Boris Johnson.
His earnest attempts at connecting with voters saw him taking awkward, unpolished selfies with members of the public that earned considerable online attention.
He was later named a 'weird crush' by viewers of the televised Tory leadership debates, particularly as he removed his tie during one broadcast – in order to, he later said, escape from the 'alternate reality' of the TV studio.
During the 2020 London mayoral race, in which he ran as an independent candidate, Mr Stewart launched a bizarre campaign in which he tried to invite himself into voters' homes to see how the capital's denizens live.
Prior to his political career Mr Stewart served briefly as an officer in the British Army, but quit the armed forces to study at Oxford, where he briefly tutored Princes William and Harry.
He then joined the Foreign Office in the late 1990s, working at the British Embassy in Jakarta, Indonesia, before serving as the British Representative to Montenegro in the aftermath of the Kosovo War.
Seeking solace, Mr Stewart then took leave to walk across Asia. The written chronicle of his walk across Afghanistan, The Places In Between, garnered international praise and was, rumour had it, optioned for a movie.
He became MP for Penrith and The Border in 2010 and served in the Cabinet in environment, international development and prisons positions before quitting Boris Johnson's cabinet in 2019.
Losing the Tory whip after refusing to vote for a no-deal Brexit, Mr Stewart then stood down in December of that year, and pulled out of the London mayoral race when it was delayed by the Covid pandemic.
He used his Newsnight appearance to warn the UK off of dependence on US and Chinese-owned artificial intelligence, branding the notion of British military, hospitals and businesses relying on foreign software 'terrifying'.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map
articles.content_orig:
People opposed to a congressional redistricting plan rally outside the Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City, Mo., earlier this month. David A. Lieb/AP hide caption
In a case watched across the country and as voting begins in the midterm elections, the Supreme Court blocked a congressional map in Missouri that was aimed at netting Republicans another seat in the U.S. House.
This is the third time the high court has blocked the redistricting plan that could have helped ousted Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver by increasing the number of Republican voters in his district.
The court warned that changing maps now would cause "electoral chaos." The decision requires the state use the same districts provided to voters in 2022 and 2024. That's even though a different map was used in the primaries there last month.
It comes after weeks of conflicting rulings in state courts and federal courts. Elections officials in Missouri already started mailing some absentee ballots last week using the old districts and some argued it would be too late to change them.
Missouri lawmakers passed the new map last year at the behest of Trump. It was part of his nationwide strategy to draw more GOP-leaning seats to prevent Republicans from losing the House.
Usually, states redistrict at the start of each decade. The redistricting battle set off by Trump ended with the GOP besting the Democrats by tilting about nine or 10 more districts, including Missouri's fifth district , their way. Republicans currently only hold a few seats advantage in the House.
But opponents of the new Missouri map successfully gathered citizen signatures to put it to a vote on the November ballot.
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled earlier this month that the ballot question meant the 2025 GOP-backed map never went into effect and was never law – even though it had been used in the Aug. 4 primaries. The state's high court blamed Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for proceeding with the GOP map in the primaries even though it hadn't been approved by voters.
The U.S. Supreme Court in its ruling today backed that up, noting that the state court had said in May - before the primary - that the GOP map would require voter approval before it could be used.
The U.S. Supreme Court had declined on Sept. 10 to intervene in the state court's ruling but allowed the case to continue.
Simultaneously, Republicans sued in federal court and won backing for the GOP map from a federal judge and then, last week, a federal appeals court. That sent the case back to the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled against Republican lawmakers today.
In general, Republicans argued that their map should be used because more than a million Missourians cast votes in the primary using the map. Opponents of redistricting argued voters hadn't approved the map and blamed Republican officials for dragging out the process and of trying to force through the new map.

articles.content_orig:
Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour.
The concerts scheduled for Friday and Saturday at the New England Patriots home stadium were scrapped because of the upcoming nor’easter , Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the statement said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”
The touring group said that refunds are available and that ticket holders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded.
The announcement comes amid a wider scandal for Sheeran’s “Loop” tour since one of its opening acts was forced out for voicing pro-Palestinian views.
Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour after speaking out in support for the Palestinian people at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Macklemore said he was removed at the behest of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and alleged that Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners.
Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. In a previous statement he said he did not intend to stifle Palestinian support but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium.
Macklemore’s removal prompted Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — to withdraw in protest.
A rep for Sheeran did not immediately return a request for comment. In his first concert since the scandal, Sheeran apologized for the scenario.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
On Thursday, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall.
The multiday nor’easter is expected to hit the East Coast, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island. Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people. Wind gusts are expected to peak on Saturday, reaching up to 60 mph in coastal locations.
Sheeran’s shows weren’t the only major musical events canceled due to the threat of severe weather in the North East, with the Global Citizen Festival at Central Park in New York City also pulling the plug.
“Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York and NYC Parks, to cancel this year’s Global Citizen Festival,” the organization wrote on social media .
“Safety has to come first,” Global Citizen added, noting that this is the first time the festival has been canceled in 14 years.
All Things Go , another New York City festival that was to be held at Forrest Hills Stadium in Queens this weekend, was also canceled due to the weather.
And a Friday night concert at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey by Australian rock legends AC/DC was postponed just hours before the show.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigns after investigation found sexual harassment and other wrongdoing
articles.title_zh: New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigns after investigation found sexual harassment and other wrongdoing
articles.content_orig:
Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell's resignation comes the day after N.J. Gov. Mikie Sherrill called on him to do so. She says she'll act swiftly to find a new No. 2.
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell has resigned after investigators found “credible evidence” of sexual harassment and other wrongdoing.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced his resignation at a news conference Friday afternoon after calling for him to step down while releasing the investigative report Thursday evening.
“His decision will allow us to move forward with important work serving the people of our state,” said Sherrill, who was inaugurated with Caldwell by her side in January.
“I will move swiftly and thoughtfully in choosing a new lieutenant governor who will represent my administration and the people of New Jersey with honor and integrity.”
The governor released a 61-page report from a monthlong investigation conducted by an outside law firm late Thursday afternoon. The report said Caldwell made inappropriate comments to women and violated ethics rules. Caldwell, a minister, is the former president of Centenary University.
Sherrill called for him to resign by Friday , but it was unclear whether he would listen. Caldwell denied the investigation’s findings through his attorney, who argued Caldwell was not given an opportunity to meaningfully address the accusations in the report or provide his own witnesses.
Sherrill emphasized Friday that she wanted to “make sure everyone was treated fairly and justly” and called the investigation thorough and impartial.
“After I received the report and the facts were clear, I took action right away,” Sherrill said, in what may have been a nod to earlier criticism that she didn’t confirm the investigation while it was underway. “Let me be clear: all credible allegations of misconduct must be fully investigated and addressed. In my administration, we are committed to doing what is right, not what is politically expedient.”
The investigation found Caldwell hit on a female staffer’s friend, and when she turned him down, he told the staffer that ambitious women like them needed a man in a position to help them, “but you young women are looking for young sperm.”
Caldwell denied making the comments, “but we did not find his denial credible,” the report said.
Sherrill did not have the power to fire Caldwell, so his resignation prevents potential impeachment proceedings in Trenton. The governor has 45 days to pick his replacement.
In the meantime, New Jersey Senate President Nicholas Scutari will lead the state in her absence. Sherrill traveled to campaign for Democrats in congressional races in other states earlier in the summer, leaving Caldwell in charge. But she stopped after the investigation became public knowledge.
Sherrill said she spoke to Caldwell on Thursday and texted with him on Friday, and that he resigned to let her administration continue with its agenda amid “all of the attacks from the federal government on affordability, voting rights.”
Caldwell’s attorney, Thomas Calcagni, said in a statement late Friday that his client continues to dispute the allegations in the report and would be exploring “all legal remedies” to contest its findings.
“We continue to forcefully challenge the report. Dr. Caldwell’s resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings,” Calcagni said.
As fragments of the allegations leaked out over the weeks, some of Caldwell’s friends and allies shared messages of support about his character and record of service. And while he did not speak publicly as news of the investigation surfaced, a May letter he wrote to the ethics commission forcefully denying the claims — and alleging racism — was leaked to media.
On Friday, a group of self-described Black “faith, civic, and community leaders” commended his decision to resign.
“By choosing to step down and ending this controversy, he has put the interests of the people of New Jersey and the work of our state ahead of himself,” the group said in a statement, which included U.S. Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D., Mercer), New Jersey Democratic Committee Chair LeRoy Jones, among others.
Democratic state legislators remained largely quiet before Caldwell announced his resignation, but many were relieved to see Caldwell step down.
Assemblymember Anthony Angelozzi, a Burlington County Democrat, said he was “appalled” with the findings of the report.
“The idea of using your government position for personal benefit and harassing women, as someone who has staff members who are female and a daughter, I wouldn’t want to put any woman in a compromised position like that,” he said.
Assemblymember Balivir Singh floated another Burlington County Democrat, State Sen. Troy Singleton, as an ideal replacement for Caldwell.
“You look for a person with integrity … and I would think my senator is the best,” Singh said.
As lieutenant governor, Caldwell served a dual role as the state’s top election official. With his resignation less than 40 days before the midterm election, Sherrill appointed Acting Comptroller Shirley Emehelu to serve as secretary of state on an acting basis.
“For months at this point, the Department of State team has been hard at work preparing for the upcoming elections in partnership with local and county election officials. I will make sure their work proceeds as planned,” Emehelu said.
The investigation into Caldwell was conducted by former Attorney General Christopher Porrino — who worked under former Republican Gov. Chris Christie — and his law firm. The probe had been going on since at least May.
Road crews had begun removing Caldwell’s name from state signs on I-95 as of Friday, but the scandal is still likely to dominate New Jersey politics for the foreseeable future.
Christine Giordano Hanlon, chair of the New Jersey GOP, called Sherrill’s handling of the investigation a “failure.”
“Caldwell’s resignation is not accountability for everything that happened before it,” she said. “There are many more questions that will need to be answered.”
Sherrill said the report “lays out a pattern and practice of long-term concerning behavior.” She said her decision shows the “culture change” she has pushed for in Trenton.
“What was so important to me was to make sure that if there are substantiated claims of sexual harassment and ethics violations, that I, as the leader of the government, handle that,” she said.
“There has been a culture in Trenton, probably since the birth of our nation, to sweep this under the rug,” she said. “You can speak to numerous people who’ve worked in the statehouse for decades who felt this day would never come, that allegations would never be taken seriously, action would never be taken, and victims would just have to either quit their job or move on.”
According to the report, less than a month after being spoken to and given training on workplace conduct and ethics, and four days after he was told about the investigation, Caldwell tried to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating.
Caldwell’s attorney said the lieutenant governor forwarded the employee’s resume and did not disclose the two had a personal relationship.
The report also details comments Caldwell allegedly made about wanting a “first lady.” One staffer said he asked her to find him someone and another recalled him suggesting that he would need a wife in order to run for governor and to let him know if she comes across someone suitable. Caldwell admitted to making comments to staffers about wanting a “first lady” but said he wasn’t serious and other people in the office made similar kinds of jokes, the report said.

The report comes as the prime minister, as well as UAE and US officials, deny allegations made in a Haaretz report that MBZ warned Netanyahu of a major Hamas attack in the days before Oct. 7, 2023.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did not disclose an alleged warning from the UAE president that Hamas was planning a major attack during a Gaza security meeting held on October 1, 2023, six days before the October 7 massacre, The New York Times reported on Friday.
The report cited five former Israeli security officials, who further told the NYT that Netanyahu rejected suggestions from his security chiefs to strike Hamas leaders in Gaza who were directing terror attacks in the West Bank, saying instead that Israel should maintain calm amid a potential diplomatic agreement with Saudi Arabia.
According to the report, Netanyahu believed the Saudi-Israeli deal to be imminent, worrying that any IDF operations in Gaza would derail such a deal.
The NYT report follows an investigation published by Haaretz on September 8 alleging that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ) warned Netanyahu that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel in the days prior to the October 7 attack, with three foreign sources saying that the prime minister dismissed the threat.
Netanyahu has denied the allegations, with the prime minister saying on September 9 that he instructed his lawyers to issue a libel lawsuit against Haaretz and the journalist who covered the story, Shlomi Eldar, according to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).
UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan looks on shortly after being greeted by President German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, at Villa Borsig on September 10, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. (credit: Omer Messinger/Getty Images)
"A thorough examination not only of the prime minister's call log, but also of the records of entries into the Prime Minister's Office during this period, does not show any entry of the Emirati representative into the Prime Minister's Office," the PMO said of the allegations, accusing it of being part of a "sinister plot with clear political timing, as part of the Left's election campaign," adding at the time that there would be "more such false plots."
The UAE also rejected the claims made in the Haaretz report, with an official UAE source told the state-owned Abu Dhabi English-language newspaper The National on Sunday that "the UAE discusses security matters with other countries through the relevant bodies, and does not discuss details of this kind at the level of the leaders of the countries."
Two sources from the United States have also weighed in on the Haaretz investigation, telling The Jerusalem Post on September 9 that the Biden administration was unaware of any specific warning from the UAE before October 7 that Hamas was planning a major attack.
Shir Perets, Tzvi Jasper, Idan Kweller, and Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Who is in the WNBA playoffs? Bracket, matchups now set
articles.title_zh: Who is in the WNBA playoffs? Bracket, matchups now set
articles.content_orig:
From the Connecticut Sun's heartfelt goodbye to Los Angeles Sparks legend Nneka Ogwumike's final game , the WNBA's 2026 regular-season finale was an emotional one. But now, it's time to wipe those tears. The playoffs are here.
Although the Sparks and Sun were long eliminated from the postseason, their Thursday night matchups were still key for the standings. For every team other than the Minnesota Lynx, Dallas Wings and New York Liberty, seeding was still on the line.
Can the Lynx return to their dynastic roots? Will the Las Vegas Aces claim their fourth WNBA title in five years and go back-to-back again? Is Golden State Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase going to supersede owner Joe Lacob's mandate to win a championship in the first five years of the team's existence and do it in two? Can the Indiana Fever's All-Star core bring home their first league title since 2012? Or will the champion be a wild card like the young Washington Mystics and Dallas Wings or championship-less Atlanta Dream?
The road to determining those answers begins when the playoffs officially tip off on Sunday, Sept. 27, and each team's respective journeys will be impacted by variables that have now been determined; including who drew who in the matchups, and which teams will start with homecourt advantage.
USA TODAY has you covered with all the details. Here's everything you need to know:
The Lynx clinched the No. 1 seed back on Tuesday, and ended the regular season with a dominant 86-66 win over the Indiana Fever. They'll have home court advantage throughout the entire playoffs, starting with Game 1 of the first round against the New York Liberty.
On Thursday night, Golden State needed a win over the Sparks or for the Aces to lose to secure the No. 2 seed. It seemed like neither would happen, until the Sparks fell in a disastrous collapse to spoil Ogwumike's final WNBA game. The Valkyries secured the No. 2 spot and will have home court advantage in the first round against the Wings.
The Aces are a top-3 seed, just like they were last season − but this time it didn't take a historic winning streak to close the regular season. They'll have home court advantage in the first round against the Fever after beating the Phoenix Mercury in their regular-season finale on Thursday.
The Dream finished the regular season by losing one of their final 10 games, and their sole loss in that span was a month ago. Atlanta clinched the No. 4 spot on Wednesday and will have home court advantage against the Mystics in the first round.
The Mystics secured their first-round date with the Dream by beating the Chicago Sky 101-93 on Thursday night, ending their season on a similar note to Atlanta's with one loss in their final eight games.
Indiana had a chance at the No. 5 seed if it won and the Mystics had lost, but the Fever will instead face the Aces without home court advantage in the first round. Luckily, they won't have to start the postseason without starting center Aliyah Boston, who exited their regular-season finale in what coach Stephanie White said postgame was just a precaution due to a "flareup."
Dallas clinched the No. 7 spot on Wednesday as it beat the Seattle Storm. The Wings were the final team to secure a spot in the postseason. Paige Bueckers will compete in her first WNBA postseason.
The Liberty also clinched their spot on Wednesday, securing a 2024 WNBA Finals rematch as they ended the season with back-to-back losses against the Dream. Although it's a tough draw, the Liberty had a 2-1 edge in the regular-season series against the Lynx and MVP candidate Breanna Stewart can never be counted out.

Previously, you could tap on a message bubble to see the sent time, read receipts, and RCS lock icon. Meanwhile, swiping left would let you send a direct reply.
A redesign today changes all that. To see timestamps, you can now swipe left anywhere in a conversation. This also shows the RCS encryption status. Being able to see all times instead of having to tap the bubbles individually is an improvement.
To reply to a message, you now have to swipe right on the bubble. Some amount of precision is required. You can still tap the message to see the read receipts.
As of today, the most widely rolled out design appears to be the old two-circle look instead of the single version that has been in testing for ages. In fact, in a real show of inconsistency, the new design widely appears on an individual message’s Details page and might also show up on the homepage.
Google changing the swipe behavior is likely the biggest disruption today. When you tap on a message, Messages will briefly have the timestamps peek out as a hint about the new behavior.

Connie Britton and Kyle Chandler's Tami and Eric Taylor were the foundation of "Friday Night Lights." Vince Bucci / Getty Images
“Friday Night Lights,” the beloved series about Texas high school football, was the highest-ranked sports-related TV show on The New York Times’ Top 100 list of the best shows of the 21st century .
“Friday Night Lights” finished at No. 14. The Times’ Top 100 list was released throughout the week and was topped by No. 1 “Breaking Bad.”
“Friday Night Lights,” airing from 2006 to 2011, “didn’t get the respect it deserved,” Times TV critic Mike Hale said. “No show has been more poignantly realistic about the lives of American teenagers, and few have showcased better acting.”
The show centers on coach Eric Taylor (Kyle Chandler) and his wife, Tami (Connie Britton). It also features standout performances from future Hollywood stars, including Michael B. Jordan and Jesse Plemons.
Other notable sports shows to make the Top 100:
No. 75, “Ted Lasso”: This is the zeitgeist-claiming “fish out of water” story of the American college football coach (Jason Sudeikis) transplanted to the glitzy, competitive world of English football. Despite the show’s “sunny reputation,” Times critic Jeremy Egner wrote, the characters’ “confronting and eventual conquering of darkness gave a very funny sports comedy surprising depth and gravity and a kind of soul-nourishing power in the dark days of the pandemic.”
No. 81, “The Queen’s Gambit”: Is chess a sport? Absolutely. “The actress Anya Taylor-Joy employs her watchful gaze and fierce intelligence to carry us through the complicated journey of a natural-born genius who is also a fanatical competitor, a pill-popping addict and, ultimately, a lost soul finding her purpose in knights and bishops,” Times critic Leah Greenblatt said.
No. 90, “Eastbound & Down”: Danny McBride plays a supremely overconfident former MLB pitcher trying to reclaim his glory and navigate his place in the world. “A fizzling 40-ounce bottle of pure hubris, McBride’s portrait of unrepentant obnoxiousness knocks it out of the park,” Times TV critic James Poniewozik said.
And, while not sports shows, worth noting:
No. 29, “Key & Peele”: The sketch-comedy series earned rave reviews from “Breaking Bad” star Bryan Cranston, specifically for its legendary sketch where Key and Peele introduced themselves as a range of college football players, gently poking fun at NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” player-introduction tradition: Hingle McCringleberry.
No. 31, “Survivor”: Is this a sports show? Well, it certainly is about competition. There is a range of physical contests, and there is a winner. At a minimum, sports-adjacent.

articles.title_orig: White House television pool resumes after banned news outlets regain access
articles.title_zh: White House television pool resumes after banned news outlets regain access
articles.content_orig:
Trump’s media ban resulted in an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the UN general assembly
The primary White House television pool has resumed filming administration events after a court ruling temporarily overturned a Trump administration ban on CNN a day earlier.
In an unprecedented move, the pool – which also includes NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News – ceased recording and transmitting White House footage on Monday, in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico, which had been banned by Trump from the building over what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
The decision meant that, for much of this week, there was no high-quality pool footage of White House events and the president’s movements, though some smaller outlets attempted to provide coverage.
With the pool still inactive on Thursday afternoon, that meant that a significant presidential event, a summit with Xi Jinping, China’s president, did not receive video coverage on the leading television networks. ABC had been listed as the TV pooler for the day, but held off until the network received assurances that CNN would be let back into the pool.
Tensions between the media and the administration were further exacerbated on Thursday evening when journalists for CNN and MS Now were denied access to the White House state dinner in honor of Xi. The journalists were blocked despite a ruling earlier in the day from a federal judge who granted a request by CNN, MS Now and Politico to force the White House to restore their access for the next two weeks while the case plays out.
Although television networks remain apprehensive, a producer for CBS News confirmed that the network would be serving as the TV pooler for the day as scheduled, according to an internal note obtained by the Guardian.
“The plan is to return covering the President in a normal capacity with a full crew,” the note read, with the pool covering Trump and Xi arriving at the South Portico for tea and a tour of the National Archives.
Pamela Brown, a CNN anchor, told viewers on Friday morning: “CNN’s access to the White House has been restored, and the TV pool appears to be functioning as normal.”
The resumption ends – for now – an extraordinary standoff between the US’s biggest media companies and the Trump administration that led to an effective TV blackout of coverage of the president during the United Nations general assembly.
For decades, the five networks have shared the cost and responsibility of providing footage of the president that is carried by news outlets worldwide.
Pool subscribers had originally received a note on Monday from Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who is now serving as the TV pool chair, saying that it would cease operations. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” he wrote in a memo. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.”

articles.title_orig: EU vows to defend its stand against X after the US backs a court challenge from Elon Musk - ABC News
articles.title_zh: EU vows to defend its stand against X after the US backs a court challenge from Elon Musk - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The European Union says it's ready to defend a 120 million euro fine issued to social media platform X
BRUSSELS -- The European Union's executive arm said Friday it's prepared to defend a 120 million euro ($137 million) fine against the social media platform X after the U.S. government threw its support behind a legal effort by Elon Musk this week to have the case dismissed.
The European Commission fined X late last year for breaches of the bloc’s landmark digital regulations, stoking tensions with Washington.
The U.S. Justice Department said Thursday that it had filed an application to support X's bid to have the case annulled at the European Union's General Court. It was the second time in three months that the Justice Department has intervened to defend a company owned by Musk.
In July, the Justice Department filed a motion to intervene in a civil rights lawsuit that alleges Musk’s xAI is illegally running dozens of natural gas turbines to power a $20 billion AI data center in Mississippi.
In that case, the NAACP and other groups said xAI failed to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools and churches — creating health risks for families in North Mississippi and nearby Memphis and violating the federal Clean Air Act.
Trump and the world's richest businessman appeared to dial down a war of words that stunned Washington and Wall Street alike last year after Musk called Trump's tax breaks and spending cuts a “disgusting abomination.”
Musk on Thursday evening attended a state dinner held by Trump honoring China’s leader Xi Jinping , along with other tech titans.
The EU fine against X, which followed a two-year investigation , was the first penalty issued under the bloc's digital regulations governing online content. Regulators said X’s blue checkmarks broke the rules because they involved“deceptive design practices” and could expose users to scams and manipulation.
European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Friday that it is the EU’s “sovereign right” to draft legislation aimed at protecting its citizens.
“We are enforcing our legislation objectively, transparently and with a solid case,” he told reporters. “We are ready to defend our position in court. We have a lot of evidence at our disposal, and it will be for the court to decide as always.”
The commission is the top enforcer of the 27-nation EU's Digital Services Act , which requires tech companies to clean up their online platforms under threat of hefty financial penalties.
But the rulebook has become a flashpoint with the Trump administration, and U.S. officials have criticized it as amounting to online censorship.
The Justice Department warned that the fine, if upheld, “may have significant implications” for U.S. online platforms and other companies providing digital services in the EU.
Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in Thursday's statement that the "European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,”
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” he said.
When asked whether the Justice Department had informed the commission that it intended to back Musk, Regnier said: “We do not need to be informed about anything.”
He said the commission doesn't expect the case to hurt broader relations between Brussels and Washington, notably in talks to mitigate the damage of Trump administration tariffs.
“From our perspective, nothing will change because of a DSA case,” he said.
AP Business Writer Kelvin Chan contributed to this report from London.

articles.title_orig: Owner of facility where Presley Gerber died had an alleged drug-related criminal history
articles.title_zh: Owner of facility where Presley Gerber died had an alleged drug-related criminal history
articles.content_orig:
New details about the recovery facility where Presley Gerber died are putting its founder’s past under scrutiny. Reza Nabavi , the psychologist who founded Resolutions Living in Santa Monica, California, had two drug-related arrests in 2002 and initially encountered problems obtaining professional registration because of his criminal history, according to records cited by Page Six and other outlets. California Board of Psychology records also document later disciplinary proceedings involving Nabavi.
The revelations have emerged days after Gerber, the 27-year-old son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, died on September 20, 2026. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner recorded his place of death as a rehabilitation facility but has not yet established an official cause of death.
Santa Monica police are investigating the death as a suspected overdose . Authorities have said there is currently no indication of foul play, while toxicology testing is expected to play a key role in determining what happened.
Nabavi is a licensed clinical psychologist and founder of Resolutions Therapeutic Services. His professional biography says he specializes in substance-use disorders, mood and anxiety disorders, process addictions, and co-occurring conditions.
But recently resurfaced records have drawn attention to events from more than two decades ago. According to official documents reviewed by Page Six and subsequently reported by TMZ and Infobae , Oakland police arrested Nabavi in February 2002, when he was 25 years old. Officers reportedly discovered him asleep in a vehicle in an area authorities associated with frequent narcotics and prostitution activity.
A 15-year-old girl was reportedly inside the vehicle. According to accounts of the records, she told police she did not know Nabavi well and was under the influence of methamphetamine.
Police reportedly found methamphetamine, marijuana, a firearm, ammunition, and a hunting knife while searching the vehicle.
In May 2002, Nabavi pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor controlled-substance possession charge and received 36 months of probation, according to reports based on the records.
Later that month, he was arrested again following an incident in which he allegedly agreed to sell methamphetamine to an informant. Authorities reportedly recovered methamphetamine, marijuana, and a glass pipe during the subsequent search.
Nabavi again pleaded no contest to misdemeanor possession of a controlled substance and received another 36-month probation sentence, according to Infobae’s review of the records.
The decades-old cases later became relevant when Nabavi sought professional registration in psychology.
Nabavi reportedly applied to the California Board of Psychology for professional registration in 2004. His application was denied, according to reports citing board documents. The cited reasons included his criminal conviction, use of a controlled substance, and conduct considered relevant to professional psychology practice. Another application was denied in 2005.
He eventually obtained registration as a psychological assistant in January 2006. The following month, that registration was revoked, but the revocation was stayed while Nabavi was placed under conditions that reportedly included supervision, substance testing, and participation in a drug and alcohol recovery program.
Nabavi ultimately became registered as a psychologist in December 2006 after complying with the conditions imposed on him, according to the records cited in recent reporting.
California Board of Psychology meeting minutes confirm that Nabavi later petitioned for termination of his probation in May 2008. His current psychology license is reported as active through June 30, 2028.
The distinction between a rehabilitation center and a sober-living residence has become an important part of the Presley Gerber case. Although the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner classified Gerber’s place of death as a rehabilitation facility, California authorities have reportedly said Resolutions Living is not licensed as a residential substance-use disorder treatment facility.
The California Department of Health Care Services told TMZ that it has no record of Resolutions operating as a licensed substance-use disorder residential treatment facility in Santa Monica. Based on available information, the agency said the program appeared to operate as a sober-living environment or recovery residence.
Sober-living residences can operate without the same state license required for facilities providing residential substance-use treatment.
Resolutions Therapeutic Services separately advertises outpatient mental-health and addiction services. Its website identifies Nabavi as its founder and executive clinical director.
Gerber reportedly arrived at the Santa Monica facility on the evening of Saturday, September 19, only hours before his death.
The Los Angeles Times reported that Santa Monica police received calls concerning both a cardiac arrest and an overdose at Resolutions Living the following morning. Officers responded at approximately 9:35 a.m., and Gerber was pronounced dead shortly afterward.
Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death, including the possible source of drugs involved in the suspected overdose. However, the medical examiner has deferred the official cause and manner of death while toxicology testing is completed.
Although law enforcement is investigating an apparent or suspected overdose, an overdose has not yet been officially established as Gerber’s cause of death.
There is also currently no public finding that Nabavi or Resolutions Living caused Gerber’s death.
Before his death, Gerber had discussed his experiences with mental health and substance use .
In one of his final social media posts, he documented undergoing an ibogaine treatment as part of his efforts to address addiction. The model had also spoken publicly about depression and substance-use struggles and had launched a social media series focused on mental health.
Gerber was the only son of Crawford and Rande Gerber and the older brother of model and actress Kaia Gerber. He had established his own modeling career, working with major fashion brands including Calvin Klein and Dolce & Gabbana.
His family has asked for privacy following his death.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo warns a 'paradise of machines' could undermine humanity on his France visit
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo warns a 'paradise of machines' could undermine humanity on his France visit
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV and French President Emmanuel Macron attend a joint statement at the Élysée Palace in Paris, Friday. Teresa Suarez/AP hide caption
PARIS — Pope Leo XIV warned Friday that a "paradise of machines" risked undermining humanity as he opened a trip to France by posing fundamental questions about what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence, a nuclear arms race and other threats to life itself.
Leo raised existential concerns about scientific progress, life and human rights during his opening speech to President Emmanuel Macron and authorities at the Élysée Palace and then to diplomats and United Nations employees at the headquarters of UNESCO, the U.N. culture and education organization.
With wars plaguing Europe and the Middle East, he reaffirmed the Vatican's opposition to nuclear weapons and said the nuclear deterrence doctrine was "mistaken" since it was just fueling a new arms race.
"Peace is not a balance of power; rather, it is built day by day through dialogue and justice," he said.
Leo has an intense four days in France, where the Catholic Church has lost ground on influencing ethical issues given the strict approach to secularism that is enshrined in the French Constitution.
Church bells tolled across the country when Leo's charter flight landed at Paris' Orly airport, and more than a million people are expected to turn out to see him. They lined the streets of the capital as Leo's motorcade passed by, underscoring the surprising level of interest in Leo's visit, the first official state visit by a pope in 18 years.
Macron said Leo's visit brings "a source of hope" to many French people.
"France stands on the side of peace, effective multilateralism, respect for international law and the United Nations Charter ... because every life has equal value, and all peoples must be defended," he said.
For Macron, who is barred from seeking a third term in May elections, hosting the American pope is something of a capstone. Pope Francis had refused repeatedly to make a proper state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and pointedly refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame cathedral in 2024.
"For a president of the republic as Macron, who is at the end of his mandate, it can be important to be aside the pope and to capture a part of his popularity," said Charles Mercier, director of history and sociology of Catholicism studies at Paris EPHE university.
With seven months left in his term, Macron's approval ratings are near record lows, driven by anger over the rising cost of living and criticism of France's growing debt and deficit and deteriorating public services.
Smiling broadly as Leo spoke French, Macron thanked the pope for visiting, saying: "You are here with us for an extended visit, giving us your time, and that is moving."
The Rev. Aristide Ahidote, from Ivory Coast, was among those who planned to attend the pope's vespers service in Notre Dame later Friday. "God has given us a pope with vigor and strength," he said.
While acknowledging the French church has declined in popularity, Ahidote said "it still has small remnants and these small remnants have been edifying for me."
Unlike Francis, who liked to travel to small Catholic communities far from Rome, Leo has been keen to emphasize and reawaken Europe's Christian roots. He is seeking to push the church's message about the value and dignity of human life in a country where the right to abortion was enshrined in the constitution in 2024, and where lawmakers recently gave final approval to a bill allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication.
The French Catholic hierarchy strongly opposed the measures, in keeping with Catholic teaching that human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death.
In his speech to Macron and other government and diplomatic authorities, Leo reminded France of its "deep Christian roots" and called especially for the French to remember that the right to life is the "indispensable foundation of every other human right."
His concern about the dignity of human life and humanity as a whole extended to the threats posed by artificial intelligence.
"The paradox has become increasingly evident: while 'intelligence' is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognize the inalienable dignity of human persons, whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and, when deemed no longer productive, are rejected and discarded," he said.
From the very start of his pontificate, Leo has identified AI as one of the greatest challenges facing humanity. He dedicated his first encyclical to the topic, "Magnificent Humanity," calling for robust regulation and for AI developers to work for the common good rather than profit.
Leo also appealed to AI developers and political leaders responsible for regulating them to slow down, an appeal that several top AI companies seem to have taken to heart in recently.
"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment and the capacity to acknowledge the moral good," he said.
Speaking to reporters en route to Paris, Leo said he was pleased that his message was being heard and said he hoped the dialogue that the Vatican had initiated with tech companies would continue.
"And I think from their perspective, many of them, they're very much open to looking for ways of making sure that AI does not displace or ultimately destroy humanity, but rather than be a tool for human beings," he said. "Good things are beginning at least."

articles.title_orig: Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style "charm" housing an AI agent
articles.title_zh: Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style "charm" housing an AI agent
articles.content_orig:
Meta is creating a tiny, portable Muse Charm device for carrying around the company's AI agent, chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has announced.
Produced by Meta's new design team, led by former Apple design chief Alan Dye, the device resembles an Apple Watch but with a small lanyard instead of a strap.
A customisable cartoon character occupies the entire two-inch screen, prompting comparisons to an AI-powered Tamagotchi .
This avatar acts as the cutesy embodiment of the Muse AI agent the company launched earlier this month, billed as a "personal assistant" that can automate daily admin such as writing emails and booking appointments, rather than just answering questions.
The Muse Charm features a fingerprint sensor in the corner that users can tap to start talking to the AI, with a built-in 5G modem for Wi-Fi-less internet access. There also appears to be a small camera, allowing the agent to take in information about the user's surroundings.
Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg teased the product, set to go on sale ahead of the Christmas holidays, during the company's annual Meta Connect showcase, which also saw the launch of two new smart glasses .
"We've packed a lot of technology into this little guy," Zuckerberg said in his keynote. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The avatar can be set to a menagerie of characters, from a Muse mascot known as "Jolly" to an anthropomorphic mango, a labradoodle and a piece of toast wearing sunglasses.
Combined with playing into Gen Z's love for bag charms and Labubu-style plushies , the device seems to be pitched at a younger demographic, who are already more likely to see AI bots as companions rather than mere helpers .
Meta's Muse AI has been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since its launch in early September, according to Sensor Tower data, and is set to be added to Meta smart glasses over the coming months.
The company does not have the best track record when it comes to handling private and sensitive information.
Meta Glasses have faced backlash for being used to film people – especially women – without their consent, and for sharing private videos captured by users with subcontractors in Kenya as part of training Muse AI.
These issues may be compounded by adding an AI agent into the mix and giving it eyes and ears. In the two weeks since its launch, Muse AI has already been accused of reading users' private messages , attempting to hack their Gmail and nudging them to share their passport information and bank account details .
Using cuteness as a way to encourage users to adopt a product they might otherwise be sceptical of is not new . Robotics companies have been following a similar playbook in recent years, with launches including fluffy robots that clip onto a handbag and emotionally intelligent AI pets .

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.
